records.title: Companion Weather
records.desc:
A record that sneaks up on you. On paper, an album built around songs about current and past pets sounds like it might drift toward sentiment, whimsy, or novelty. But this one doesn’t. Instead, it lands in a far rarer place — tender, strange, bruised, funny in spots, and quietly devastating in the way only the most personal records can be.

What makes Companion Weather work is that it understands a truth most people don’t say out loud: animals are never just animals. They become roommates, witnesses, minor gods of the domestic world. They watch us unravel, recover, fall in love, lose people, change houses, change years, and become versions of ourselves we never meant to be. They sit in the background of our lives until one day we realize they were never in the background at all. This album knows that. Every song feels less like a sketch of a pet and more like a weather report from a life once shared.

There’s something deeply 1970s about the emotional temperature here. The record feels lived-in rather than manufactured — warm tape hiss, fading light, old furniture, worn sleeves, and that particular late-night honesty that only shows up when nobody is trying to impress anyone. It doesn’t overreach. It doesn’t beg for tears. It just tells the truth softly enough that the sadness has room to breathe. That restraint gives the whole thing weight.

And that’s really the secret of Companion Weather: it isn’t just about cats and dogs and beloved companions, though they are its heart. It’s about memory. Routine. Grief. The shape of a house after someone — or something — is gone. The strange dignity of everyday love. The bowl in the corner. The sound in the hallway that isn’t there anymore. The way devotion can make even the smallest life feel mythic.

At its best, the album feels like a stack of old snapshots left near a turntable during a storm. It’s intimate without becoming precious, melancholic without collapsing under its own sadness, and affectionate without ever turning cute. That’s a difficult balance to strike, but Companion Weather finds it. The result is a record that feels less like a concept album and more like a real emotional climate — a little sun, a little rain, a little ghost in the room.

Companion Weather isn’t an album about pets in the simple sense. It’s about the emotional weather they leave behind — and the lives we measure, however quietly, by who once waited for us at the door.

records.title: Spanish For Night Owls
records.desc:
Spanish For Night Owls is less a lesson than a seduction.
It lives in that strange, beautiful hour when the city softens, the lights blur, and everything starts to feel a little more cinematic.

Built on warm Spanish guitar, smoked-out beats, late-night jazz textures, and vocals that drift between intimacy and mystery, the record feels like a whispered conversation on a rooftop at 1:37 a.m. There’s romance here, but it’s not sweet. It’s moodier than that. More knowing. More electric. Like neon on wet pavement, radio static in the distance, and a language you feel before you fully understand it.

This is music for insomniacs, lovers, smokers, wanderers, and anyone who’s ever learned more from the night than they did during the day.

"Spanish For Night Owls" -  doesn’t ask for perfect fluency.

It asks you to Stay Awake.

records.title: There’s Music In Dem Darn Hills
records.desc:
Historic field recordings collide with contemporary production—past and present stitched together with a cold, steady hand. This isn’t nostalgia. It’s excavation: degraded voices, distant rooms, damaged tape, and fragments that were never meant to outlive the moment.

Each track lands like evidence—part document, part séance—where modern drums act as a heartbeat beneath something older that won’t stay quiet. You can hear the air in the room, the warble of the reel, the ghost of a sentence cut off mid-thought. Memory becomes texture. Silence becomes threat. The closer you listen, the more you listen, the recording are listening back.

Headphones recommended.  The past isn’t resonating... It’s waking up.

records.title: Venus In Spurs
records.desc: From the vibrant streets of San Francisco comes Venus In Spurs, an alt-rock band that merges the gritty edge of the Velvet Underground with the experimental flair of Can. Led by the visionary Scott Burgess, the band's sound is a kaleidoscope of raw emotion and innovative rhythms. Bassist Raul Vargas is the heartbeat of their music, crafting rich, catchy bass tones that drive the band's punchy and distinctive groove. Drummer Greg Piper, a renowned figure in the Bay Area music scene, breaks tradition with his cutting-edge electronic drum set, infusing a modern twist into their retro-inspired soundscapes. Keyboardist Steven Hubbard adds a layer of nostalgic brilliance with his keys, often reminiscent of Ray Manzarek, using vintage 1970s keyboards but favoring the versatility of his Nord Stage. Together, Venus In Spurs create a sonic experience that is both timeless and ahead of its time.

records.title: Bombing At Starbucks
records.desc:
Released in 2022, Bombing At Starbucks by A:.A:. (AKA ChemTrails, AKA Gamecat) is a three-track ambient release that drifts through globalization, corporate sameness, paranoia, and the weird psychic fog of modern life. Built from pre-9/11 field recordings and samples captured in Istanbul and other parts of Eastern Europe, the album feels less like a straightforward document and more like a haunted transmission—nostalgic, dislocated, and quietly unnerving.

There are obvious shades of Twin Peaks here, especially in “Black Lodge” and the title track, where eerie synths, degraded textures, and negative space create that Lynchian sense of dread where something feels wrong, even if you can’t fully name it. But what gives the record more weight is that it’s not just chasing mood. “No Martians” digs into the overlap between corporate mythology, conspiracy culture, and the strange fictions people start building when reality itself begins to feel overproduced.

What makes Bombing At Starbucks land is that it refuses to be just background music. It works more like a piece of sonic criticism—using atmosphere, ambiguity, and dislocation to reflect a world where branding, fear, nostalgia, and ideology have all started bleeding together. It’s eerie, thoughtful, and a little ugly in the right ways—like cultural decay turned into ambience.
